__
 
• **Haryana:**

 
 
• Delhi, the capital of India, shares its border with the state of Haryana.
 
• Haryana surrounds Delhi on three sides: in the west, north, and south.
 
• Major cities in Haryana such as Gurugram, Faridabad, and Sonipat are in close proximity to Delhi, making these areas part of the National Capital Region (NCR).
 
• The extensive connectivity between Delhi and these nearby regions in Haryana facilitates a significant socio-economic interaction.

__

• Punjab does not share a border with Delhi.
 
• It is located to the northwest of Haryana and has distinct geopolitical boundaries separated from Delhi by the state of Haryana.
 
• Punjab is renowned for its rich agricultural land, history, and Punjabi culture, but it does not have direct geographical adjacency to Delhi.
 
 
 
• **Himachal Pradesh:**
 
 
• Himachal Pradesh is a northern state known for its mountainous terrain and does not share a border with Delhi.
 
• The state's boundaries are adjacent to Punjab, Haryana, and Jammu and Kashmir, but it lies further to the north compared to Delhi.
 
• Himachal Pradesh's geographical separation from Delhi is significant enough that it does not influence Delhi's immediate socioeconomic dynamics.
 
 
 
• **Jammu and Kashmir:**
 
 
• Jammu and Kashmir, comprising the northernmost part of India, does not share a boundary with Delhi.
 
• It is separated from Delhi by a considerable distance, with the states of Punjab and Himachal Pradesh lying in between.
 
• Jammu and Kashmir's proximity to the western Himalayan range marks its distinct geographical and cultural landscape, separate from Delhi's border dynamics.

• Uttar Pradesh lies to the east of Delhi and includes important nearby cities such as Noida and Ghaziabad, which are also part of the NCR.
 
• The National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi is a significant area for India's administration, geography, and urban planning, influencing multiple surrounding states.

questions.question: McMahon Line is the boundary line between India and ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**China**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The McMahon Line is the boundary line between India and **China**.
 
• It was established as part of the Simla Convention signed in 1914 between British India and Tibet, which was not recognized by China at that time.
 
• The line is named after Sir Henry McMahon, who was the chief negotiator from the British side.
 
• The McMahon Line runs through the eastern sector of the India-China border, which is disputed by China.
 
• It is a major point of contention in the border disputes between India and China, leading to several conflicts, including the 1962 Sino-Indian War.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Simla Convention was an attempt to settle the boundaries between British India and Tibet, and to establish Tibet as an autonomous region under Chinese suzerainty.
 
• China did not accept the Simla Convention, arguing that Tibet was not a sovereign entity and hence had no authority to sign treaties.
 
• The McMahon Line has been a flashpoint in India-China relations, with both countries strengthening their military presence along the border.
 
• Despite the disputes, the McMahon Line is currently the de facto border in the eastern sector between India and China.
 
• Efforts have been made through diplomatic channels to resolve the boundary issues, but a final settlement has not yet been reached.

__
 
• **Geographical Location:** Pakistan is located to the west of India and shares a significant border with it.
 
• **Historical Context:** The India-Pakistan border was established following the partition of British India in 1947, which led to the creation of Pakistan.
 
• **Geopolitical Significance:** The relationship between India and Pakistan is of major geopolitical importance due to historical conflicts and ongoing territorial disputes, particularly over the region of Kashmir.
 
• **Border Length:** The India-Pakistan border is approximately 3,323 kilometers long and is one of the most heavily militarized borders in the world.

• The partition of British India in 1947 resulted in the creation of two independent dominions: India and Pakistan.
 
• The partition led to one of the largest mass migrations in human history and significant communal violence.
 
• The Radcliffe Line, named after its architect Sir Cyril Radcliffe, was the boundary demarcation line between India and Pakistan.
 
 
 
• **Indo-Pakistani Wars:**
 
 
• India and Pakistan have fought three major wars since their independence: in 1947, 1965, and 1971.
 
• The 1971 war led to the creation of Bangladesh, formerly East Pakistan.
 
• There have also been numerous skirmishes and border conflicts, particularly in the Kashmir region.
 
 
 
• **Kashmir Conflict:**
 
 
• The Kashmir conflict is a territorial dispute between India and Pakistan over the Kashmir region.
 
• Both countries claim the region in full but control only parts of it.
 
• The conflict has resulted in several wars and ongoing military standoffs.

• The Line of Control (LoC) is the de facto border between India and Pakistan in the region of Jammu and Kashmir.
 
• It was established following the Simla Agreement in 1972 after the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971.
 
• The LoC is highly militarized and often a site of conflict and skirmishes between the two countries.

• It serves as the easternmost tributary of the Indus River. The Bhakra Dam, constructed on the Sutlej River, facilitates irrigation and other amenities for the states of Punjab, Rajasthan, and Haryana.
 
• Under the Indus Waters Treaty between India and Pakistan, the waters of the Sutlej River are allocated to India.
 
• These waters are primarily diverted to irrigation canals within India, such as the Sirhind Canal, Bhakra Main Line, and the Rajasthan canal.
